title: Dates and deadlines with datetime
sources: Python 3.14 Standard Library: datetime, date and timedelta; reviewed 2026-10-03
masterChecklist: Standard modules: math, random, statistics, datetime, pathlib, os, sys, collections, itertools, functools
whyItMatters: Study plans, subscriptions, and reminders have due dates. Comparing strings or adding a number directly to a date is fragile; date objects and durations state the intended calculation clearly.
simpleExplanation: datetime.date represents a calendar day without a time of day. date.fromisoformat reads a YYYY-MM-DD date. datetime.timedelta represents a duration, so adding timedelta(days=7) advances the calendar date by seven days. Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta; its days attribute is the calendar-day difference. For appointments at a specific moment, use timezone-aware datetime values instead of a date-only value.
mentalModel: A date is a square on a calendar; a timedelta is a number of squares to move. Neither by itself says what time a meeting begins or which time zone it uses.
outcomes: Parse an ISO-format date into a date object.
Calculate a due date with timedelta.
Know when a date-only model is insufficient.

realWorldExample.scenario: A learning site schedules a review seven calendar days after a lesson is completed.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: Manual day-number arithmetic fails at month boundaries, and text comparisons assume a format that may not be enforced.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Validate input with date.fromisoformat, add a seven-day timedelta, and store/display an ISO date. Keep a separate timezone-aware design for actual appointment times.

workedExample.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta

completed = date.fromisoformat('2026-10-28')
review = completed + timedelta(days=7)
print(review.isoformat())
print((review - completed).days)
explanation: The input text is parsed into a date, not left as a string.
timedelta(days=7) crosses the October-to-November boundary correctly.
isoformat produces an unambiguous year-month-day display.
Subtracting the original date from the review date gives a seven-day duration.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Change the completed date to 2024-02-27 and advance by three days; observe leap-year handling.

procedure: Decide whether the requirement is a calendar date or an exact instant in a time zone.
Parse date-only input with date.fromisoformat and handle ValueError at the input boundary.
Represent the interval with timedelta rather than manipulating day numbers yourself.
Use isoformat for a clear stored or displayed date.
Test month-end and leap-year boundary cases.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding 7 to a day number manually.
commonMistakes.why: Days roll into new months and leap years.
commonMistakes.avoid: Add timedelta(days=7) to a date object.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling a date-only deadline an exact appointment instant.
commonMistakes.why: A date has no hour or timezone.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use an aware datetime when scheduling a moment across time zones.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming any date-shaped text is valid.
commonMistakes.why: A value such as 2026-02-30 cannot be parsed as a real date.
commonMistakes.avoid: Catch ValueError and show the learner which input was invalid.

lab.title: Schedule a review across a month boundary
lab.safety: Uses fictional dates in memory only.
lab.starterCode:
from datetime import date, timedelta

completed = date.fromisoformat('2026-12-29')
# Schedule the next review five calendar days later.
# Print the ISO date and elapsed number of days.
guidedSteps: Create a timedelta of five days.
Add it to the completed date.
Subtract completed from review and print the days difference.
checks: No manual month arithmetic is used.
hints: (review - completed).days is the elapsed calendar-day count.
lab.solution:
from datetime import date, timedelta

completed = date.fromisoformat('2026-12-29')
review = completed + timedelta(days=5)
print(review.isoformat())
print((review - completed).days)
lab.solutionExplanation: Adding a timedelta handles the year boundary; subtraction checks the five-day interval.
challenges: Predict the result for 2024-02-27 plus three days.
Find the bug: replace timedelta with completed.day + 5.
Experiment: subtract five days instead of adding them.

projectConnection.milestone: Store the lesson-completion date and compute a next-review date with timedelta.

assessment.explanation: Use an aware datetime for a precise scheduled instant.
